newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS - Hong Kong falls prey to Asia currency panic.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Hong Kong falls prey to Asia currency panic.

text.p: Asian currency panic filtered through the Hong Kong money market on Friday, sending interest rates skywards while currency forwards soared.
But the Hong Kong dollar remained rock solid in steady two-way trade, ignoring the ruckus just 46 days before this British colony reverts to Chinese control.

The Hong Kong dollar closed at HK$7.7385 on Friday, flat against Thursday's close and well within its unofficial trading band of one percent either side of an enforced peg of HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.

"I don't think there's a problem in Hong Kong but there's a lot of currency turmoil in Asia and there aren't many countries that aren't affected by it," said Daniel Hemmant, Asian exotic currency fund manager at Guinness Flight Asia Ltd.

Speculative concern about the Thai baht and Malaysian ringgit sparked sudden rate action in Hong Kong when Malaysia's central bank denied publicly that it had ordered banks to cease ringgit swap, or forward, transactions with foreign banks.
Hong Kong currency forwards suddenly blew out to 65 in the three-month and 100 in the six-month from more usual levels of 15 and 40 respectively, widening further in afternoon trade.
Rates also skyrocketed, responding to a sudden 100-basis point rise in the overnight rate to 6.50 percent.

The one-week Exchange Fund bill yield closed at 6.16 percent while the two-year spread to the U.S. treasury -- considered a benchmark in Hong Kong's young and thinly-traded market -- gaped to 107 points from a more usual 30.
Dealers reported intervention by the territory's de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, but it appeared to have little effect at calming the market.

"The market is very nervous," one dealer said at the close. "People are concerned there will be more attacks on the Malaysian ringgit and that they will succeed. If that happens, it won't be good for Hong Kong."

But analysts said the market action in Hong Kong was a predictable knee-jerk reaction to currency turmoil in Thailand and Malaysia, where poor economic fundamentals attracted the attention of hedge funds from overseas.
"Basically this is a knee-jerk move rather than a fundamentally-based move and it'll snap back fairly quickly," said Callum Henderson, currency analyst at MMS International.
Dealers seemed confident about the Hong Kong dollar, long considered a possible target for speculators on uncertainty associated with the switch to Chinese sovereignty on July 1.

Foreign exchange reserves of US$63.4 billion at the end of March and Hong Kong's sturdy fiscal and economic position were powerful disincentives to speculators tempted by the infectious spread of currency weakness throughout the region, dealers said.

"Who dares to touch us? Not even (George) Soros dares to touch us. Everything is well prepared," one dealer said, referring to the hedge fund speculator who forced sterling out of the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992.
Hong Kong's situation is very different from Thailand, which is weighed under with bad debt, or Malaysia, which suffers from a wide current account deficit, he said.
